svg.title: Cardioversion, defibrillation, pacemakers and ICDs
svg.desc: Two rhythm strips. On the first the shock is drawn landing exactly on an R wave, which is what synchronised means; on the second the trace is a chaotic squiggle with no R wave to wait for, so the shock cannot be synchronised and is delivered immediately. Below, the four devices and what each is for, and living with one.
svg.text: CARDIOVERSION IS SYNCHRONISED. DEFIBRILLATION IS NOT.
Synchronised means the shock waits for the R wave. With no R wave to wait for, you cannot synchronise.
CARDIOVERSION
synchronised · low energy
the shock WAITS for this R wave
There IS a pulse. A-fib with a rate she cannot
tolerate, SVT, unstable atrial flutter.
Shocking on a T wave can cause V-fib — which is
exactly what synchronising prevents.
DEFIBRILLATION
NOT synchronised · high energy
no R wave to wait for → shock NOW
There is NO pulse. V-fib, or pulseless V-tach.
The machine cannot find an R wave, so it will
refuse to fire if you leave sync on — and that
delay is the whole danger.
⚡ THE TWO IMPLANTED DEVICES
PACEMAKER
for a heart that is too SLOW
symptomatic bradycardia, complete heart block,
sick sinus. It fires when the heart does not.
ICD
for a heart that is too FAST and lethal
it watches, and shocks V-tach or V-fib.
Many are combined pacemaker and ICD.
🏠 LIVING WITH ONE
· Check the pulse daily; report a rate below the set one
· Carry the device card, always
· No MRI unless the device is MRI-conditional
· Airport security: show the card, do not linger in the arch
· Mobile phone on the OPPOSITE ear, 6 inches away
· Avoid arc welding and large running motors
· No heavy lifting or arm raising above the head for 4–6 weeks
· If an ICD fires once and she feels well: call. Fires twice, or
she feels unwell: that is 911.
· Microwaves and induction hobs are fine.
